messages.subject: Repeated-measures Designs
messages.body_plain:
G'Day S+ 
Users,

 

I am currently try 
to use a split-plot type ANOVA to analysis an unusual experimental design based 
on the examples given in the SPlus statistics Vol1 - Repeated Measures 
Design.

The experiment 
consists of a total of 42 subjects (ID) split between two 
treatments.

A maximum of 27 
repeated measurement for each subject were taken.

Some subjects 
were removed from the experiment progressively through time. i.e. 3 per 
treatment per day so by the end of the experiment there remained only 3 subjects 
per treatment.

 

The results for the 
split-plot ANOVA are below.

What I would like to 
know is where it gets the 7 degrees of freedom for time factor 
(Hours)?

I realise that this 
term doesn't appear when there are equal number of measurements as per the 
repeated-measures design example in SPlus Statistics Vol1.

 

Also if anyone can 
suggest an alternative analysis I would be interested.

 

Thanks in 
advance

Jody

that case, the help page says explicitly:

<quote>

agnes is fully described in chapter 5 of Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990). 
Compared to other agglomerative clustering methods such as hclust, agnes 
has the following features: (a) it yields the agglomerative coefficient 
(see agnes.object) which measures the amount of clustering structure 
found; and (b) apart from the usual tree it also provides the banner, a 
novel graphical display (see plot.agnes).

...

REFERENCES:

Kaufman, L. and Rousseeuw, P. J. (1990). Finding Groups in Data: An 
Introduction to Cluster Analysis. Wiley, New York.

</quote>

I suggest you look at the reference.

--sundar

messages.subject: Re: [R/S] strange solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Erin: 

     A cleaner way is to pass "n2" to "outer" as a "..." argument, as 
in the following modification of your code: 

boot1 <- function(y,method="f",p=1) {
n1 <- length(y)
n2 <- n1*p
n3 <- n2 - 1
a <- 0.5*(outer(1:n3,1:n3,function(x,y, n2.){n2. - pmax(x,y)}, n2.=n2))
return(a)
}

y1 <- c( 9,  8, 7, 3, 6)

boot1(y=y1,p=4)

     The use of "assign" like this might be called "dirty programming", 
in the sense that any object "n2" in working directory will be 
overwritten without warning by the function "boot1", and then "boot1" 
leaves the "n2" garbage after it's done.  If you aren't aware of this 
side effect, you could get unpredictable problems with any other use of 
"n2" in the working directory. 

     The difference arises because of differences in the way R and 
S-Plus "scope" variable names.  This is described in the "R Language 
Definition" manual;  search for "scope" and "scoping" or do an R Site 
Search for terms like this at "www.r-project.org". 

     Passing the "n2" as an argument as I did in the above code seemed 
to work for me just now in S-Plus 6.2 and R 1.9.1 under Windows 2000. 

     Hope this helps. 
     Spencer Graves

messages.subject: Re: [R] Re: [R/S] strange solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andy: 

     Thanks.  However, this creates an incompatibility between S-Plus 
and R.  Including 'assign("n2", n1*p, frame=1)' in "boot1" in R 1.9.1 
produces, 'Error in assign("n2", n1 * p, frame = 1) :

   unused argument(s) (frame ...)'.  The problem, as I'm sure you are 
aware, is that "frame" is an argument of "assign" in S-Plus but not R.  
The following uses "assign" in S-Plus (where it is needed) but not in R 
(where it is not needed). 

boot1. <- function(y,method="f",p=1) {
n1 <- length(y)
n2 <- n1*p
if(is.null(version$language))assign("n2", n1*p, frame=1)
n3 <- n2 - 1
a <- 0.5*(outer(1:n3,1:n3,function(x,y){n2 - pmax(x,y)}))
return(a)
}

You can convert the column to a timeDate class after you read the data.
"20 May 2004 14:18:09".

x <- read.table("path/to/data.csv", sep = ",", header = TRUE)
x$date <- timeDate(as.character(x$date), "%d %m %y %H:%M:%S")

See ?timeDate and ?class.timeDate.

--sundar

messages.subject: Re: Fitting the matrix
messages.body_plain:
Depends on how you want the nonlinear part to be fitted.  If 
you want `smooth' curves that fit the data without knowing the functional form, 
you can use something like gam(z ~ x + s(y),...).  If you have some 
functional form in mind, and it's linear in parameters, then plain lm() will 
do.  If the functional form is not linear in the parameters, I believe you 
can use nls() with partially linear fit.

 

Andy

UNH: Dept. of Mathematics & Statistics:
Fall 2004

MATH 969
Topics:
Spatial Statistics

Description

Spatial Statistics is the study of models and methods for
the analysis of data that is collected in space.  Most
often space means the 2-dimensional geographic space
(geospatial) or a 3- dimensional space (atmosphere,
ocean, subterranean).  Space can also be the two or
three-dimensional image space of image analysis.
Classical statistical theory is based on the
cross-sectional paradigm of independently sampled data.
In spatial statistics observations in close spatial
proximity tend to be correlated, leading to much more
complicated stochastic models than in classical statistics.
In this course we will discuss methods for two types of
spatial data:
(1) point referenced data (or continuous space).  These
include so-called geostatistical methods of correlation
structure (or variogram) estimation, and spatial interpolation,
typically from a spatially irregular set of stations to a
regular grid.
(2) Areal data, or so-called lattices, such as in county
averages, remote sensing grids, image analysis.  Here we
construct a graph of the neighbor relations which the model
fitting is based on.  We discuss Markov random field models
and similar spatial autoregressions.
Both types of data may be embedded in a regression set-up
and for this we discuss the modern methods of Bayesian
hierarchical modeling and analysis that have been most
successful in this context.  As a by-product, students
will learn a fair bit of Bayesian statistics and related
modern computational methodologies, such as simulation –
based inference, Gibbs sampling, and Markov chain Monte
Carlo (MCMC) methods.
We will also discuss issues and methods related to spatial
misalignment (or modified areal unit problem), multivariable
spatial data (coregionalization) and spatial-temporal data.

Course Organization

Instructor:     Ernst Linder,   603-862 - 2687     elinder at math.unh.edu
Text:   (Required):  Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data
 by S. Banerjee, B.P. Carlin, and A.E. Gelfand.  2004 Chapman Hall/CRC Press,

Software:       We will be using the following software
-  S-Plus Version 6.2 plus the module S-Plus Spatial.
(freely available to students through UNH’s site license).
-  R and R-package GeoR  (freeware)
-  Winbugs  (freeware)

Distance Learning:      This course is offered as “FAR-VIEW”
synchronously on-line using LEARNLINC
LearnLinc is a client-server software tool being used as a
platform for Distance Education at the University of New
Hampshire. With LearnLinc, students can attend a live class
session led by an instructor using their Windows computer
system and an Internet connection. The instructor's voice,
along with course materials, are delivered to both local
and off-campus students in real time.
Learn more about FarView at www.unh.edu/farview

Prerequisites:  1)  Knowledge of intermediate statistics:
Distributions, discrete and continuous random variables,
transformation of variables (calculus based!),  bivariate
and multivariate normal distribution.
2)  Working knowledge of linear regression and analysis of
variance.
3)  Basic linear algebra: Vectors and matrices, linear spaces,
matrix multiplication, inverse of a matrix, positive definiteness.
Matrix-vector notation for linear regression and ANOVA.

Homework:       Homework assignments will be given on a regular
basis.  Most homeworks will require computer-based calculations.
One hour of computer lab will be scheduled where students can
work on homework assignment with the help of the instructor.

Final Exam:     A comprehensive final take-home exam will be
assigned during the last week of classes.  For this exam students
will be asked to perform several in-depth analyses of spatial data.

Grade Calculation:  Homework 65 %,  Final Exam:  30 %,  Participation 5%.

messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

I have encountered a problem that's driving me crazy!  I have a function
that I have been running for years without problems, but when I ran it
yesterday it killed S+.  Trying to narrow down the problem I striped down
the function to a one liner, sometimes it runs sometimes it kills S+.  Here
it is.

function(data, fac, weights = rep(1, dim(data)[1]))
{
      return(list(cat = fac, w = weights, d = dim(data)[2]))
      if(!is.data.frame(data))
            data <- as.data.frame(data)
}
When it aborts it does so with the following message.

Terminating S Session: Signal: bad address signal

Process S+6 exited abnormally with code 1 at Thu Sep  2 11:46:57 2004

What puzzles me the most is that although on most tries S+ crashes, it
doesn't all the time, sometimes it returns successfully and the returned
objects are as expected BUT it always crashes if I move the return
statement just after the if statement.  This is a 64 bit version, of course
the input objects are big, close to 3M records, but there is lots of RAM,
8Gb and it doesn't even uses 1Gb before crashing.

Here are the version and machine specs.

messages.body_plain:
thanks to all who responded.  Bill Dunlap and tech. support suggest this is
probably a bug and running a C debugger seems to confirm this.  Tech.
support will help to track it down, in the mean time I'll go back to 6.0,
the previous release for Solaris 64-bit.  By the way I never encountered
that type of problem with S+6.0!

Some people suggested trying to use, in replacement of S+ or jointly with
S+, a 64-bit version of R.  I have tried that last winter.  It wasn't easy
to install under Solaris, without the help of Brian Ripley I probably would
never have succeeded in compiling it.  But eventualy I got it to work and
my experience with it was not very good.  Since R must load all its current
project workspce in RAM it is very inconvenient when a single project has a
few very large objects associated with it.  I found that when 2 or 3 Gb are
occupied by a workspace it takes R for ever to load it up in RAM, even if a
lot of RAM is available.  Furthermore, I tested running glm on the same
object, same model, in R and S+, R took roughly twice as long to complete
and used about 10 to 20% more RAM.  That was the end of my flirt with R!  R
is probably a very good piece of software, developed by very smart and
highly dedicated people but, in my opinion, not suited yet to deal with the
Gb of data that industry throws at statisticians.

Thanks again to all who took the time to respond and I'll post a summary
whenever thech. support comes up with a definite answer, and hopefully a
patch,

messages.subject: Survival Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello, 

  

  Working in the 
pharmacokinetic area, I don't have such a big experience in survival analysis. 
For analysis purposes, I now need to get deeper into it and I would be glad to 
get some help from the list.

 

    I am 
currently working with S+6.2 under windows2000.

 

    The 
background of the analysis is patients who go into two selection periods and 
then are randomised in three arms, two are receiving drugX at two different 
doses and the last arm is a comparator.

    For 
each visit (5 visits, two before treatment and three after treatment) , the 
patient goes through an exercise that is stop when it starts to be painful. The 
time is considered as the end-point. Therefore, patients performed 5 times a 
similar exercise.

    The 
hypothesis are that under treatment the measured time is 
increased.

 

    Then 
I started with a some cox models as follow: 

    

                
TAOincl.mod3_coxph(Surv(TAO)~SLOP*INIV, # Test de l'effet de la pente et de la 
valeur basale

                                                    
data="">

                                                    
subset=VIS<=0,

                                                    
cluster(ID))

 

    In 
this specific model, TAO is the time of interest, SLOP and INIV are two 
different covariates.

    The 
data are 593 patients (ID) and 2448 observations.

    

 

Based on this background 
my questions are:

      What 
  S+ is doing when using the cluster function to weight the data? How is it 
  dealing with the different events of a single subject?

      How 
  to discriminate between two models? Not talking in terms of statistical 
  difference but mostly clinical differences? Is there any 
  relevant graphics to look at to check any potential influence of 
  covariates on the outcomes. Survival curves and residual plot have already 
  been checked.

Any help or comments 
about those two (maybe naive questions...for statisticians) questions would be 
very wellcome,

 

Thanks for your 
help,

 

Vincent

messages.subject: GW group
messages.body_plain:
Hello Storet Users:

My apologies to the group for the delay in getting back to you. The upcoming 
User Conference and the re-start of discussions for Storet 3.0 have prompted me 
back into action.
 
The initial idea for an informal ground water (GW) group was to bring together 
interested parties and brainstorm any GW specific data issues which are 
important regarding the current/future versions of Storet. These topics may 
include information on well, well construction, aquifer characteristics, GW-SW 
interaction, SIM, interaction with third-party software such as ArcView GIS, 
S-Plus, or any other GW specific attribute reporting issues/requirements.  

I encourage all who are using (or are interested in using) Storet for managing 
GW resources information to lend your professional experience and support to 
this effort.  One thing I have noticed is the high variability in the manner of 
"doing business" between different data owners. Each entity has different 
data/attribute requirements, and so has different needs and experiences. Thus, 
most have a refreshing and new insight specific to their situation, and can 
enhance each others' interaction with Storet.  I think this general quality is 
a credit to the developers of the current Storet, in spite of grumbles about 
its "generic" nature.

We hope to have a break-out session at the 2004 User's Conference in New 
Orleans in November. This will give us the opportunity to meet and discuss 
specifics. If you are interested in this session, or have any further questions 
or comments, you can contact me either by phone, email, or the listserver.

About our Storet experience at Ohio EPA:
I am a geologist in the Division of Drinking and Ground Waters at Ohio EPA. We 
have recently completed the migration of our Ambient Ground Water Monitoring 
Program data to modern Storet. Our Storet experience has led us to create a set 
of oracle tables and a Data Entry Module to house/manage those ground water 
related items not currently found in Storet, but deemed necessary for our 
program/operation.  For the most part, these items relate to programmatic 
issues, including site status and status histories, which are part of the 
sampling schedule calculations.  Also managed in this new add-on are 
miscellaneous geologic, lithologic, ArcView GIS, and other types of well and 
site attributes.

Finally,  I would like to indicate the previously interested GW folks, and 
humbly request that they re-support our combined GW effort (especially you, 
Pete):

In answer to the questions --
 
 1. For a full answer you should look at a book, for which multiple events
 is the largest chapter.  "Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox Model"
 by Therneau and Grambsch.
    The short answer is
        - this is exactly equivalent to the "working independence" model of
        generalized estimating equations (GEE). 
        - the estimate of beta does not account for the correlation, but the
        estimated variance is corrected
   
 2. There is no good answer to this.  The m-residuals are a graphical method.
In non-survival data, the equivalent question is "are scatter plots of y vs
each x sufficient to determine influence?"   Scatter plots are normally
a great help in answering such a question, but it is also clear that there
are counterexamples.

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: Re: Error in clustering procedure
messages.body_plain:
A distance matrix on 7000 objects alone takes up 187Mb.  I don't know how 
your machine is set up re swap space, but you should use your task manager 
to monitor memory usage.  Almost certainly you are running out of memory.

However, I have never seen an agglomerative clustering of 7000 objects
make sense scientifically (not that that stops the bioinformatics people).  
I think you need either to work in smaller subsets or to combine objects
into clusters before starting.

messages.subject: Re: Problem with function round
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 9 Sep 2004 asanquer at virbac.fr wrote:

> does someone could explain me the following results, which seems to be a
> bug:
> 
> round(1.275,digits=2)
> 
> The result is 1.27
> 
> and for : round(1.235,digits=2), the result is 1.24 !
> 
> I think that when rouding off a 5, the round function must go the even
>    digit. In the first example, the expected result is 1.28.

That is what it says on the help page.  However, 1.275 is not represented
exactly (only binary fractions are), so it is not rounding a five.

> print(1.275, digits=17)
[1] 1.2749999999999999

shows the internal representation is just less than 1.275 (although 
printing can introduce errors, too).

One always needs to keep in mind that computers do not do arithmetic 
exactly.

--

messages.subject: Release of CircStats Version 2.0 for S-PLUS, a library for circular statistics
messages.subject_clean: Release of CircStats Version 2.0 for S-PLUS, a library for circular statistics
messages.body_plain:
An updated version of CircStats for S-PLUS is now available at the 
bottom of the following URL:

http://statweb.calpoly.edu/lund/

CircStats is a library of functions for the analysis of circular data. 
Version 2.0 was created and tested on MS Windows machines running 
Windows 2000 and XP, and using S-PLUS 6.2 for Windows.

Below is an excerpt of the Readme file with further information 
regarding the contents of the library.

=======================================================================================
CircStats: S-PLUS Functions for Circular Statistics
           Version 2.0
           September, 2004
=======================================================================================

Function            Title
==================  ==================================================
A1                  Ratio of First and Zeroth Order Bessel Functions
A1inv               Inverse of A1
change.pt           Change Point Test
circ.aov            Circular Analysis of Variance
circ.cor            Correlation Coefficient for Angular Variables
circ.disp           Circular Dispersion
circ.lin.reg        Circular-Linear Regression
circ.mean           Mean Direction
circ.plot           Circular Data Plot
circ.range          Circular Range
circ.reg            Circular-Circular Regression
circ.summary        Circular Summary Statistics
dcard               Cardioid Density Function
deg                 Degrees
dmixedvm            Mixture of von Mises Distributions
dtri                Triangular Density Function
dvm                 von Mises Density Function
dwrpcauchy          Wrapped Cauchy Density Function
dwrpnorm            Wrapped Normal Density Function
equal.kappa.test    Test for Homogeneity of Concentration Parameters
est.kappa           Estimate Kappa
est.rho             Mean Resultant Length
I.0                 Zeroth Order Bessel Function of the First Kind
I.1                 First Order Bessel Function of the First Kind
I.p                 P-th Order Bessel Function of the First Kind
kuiper              Kuiper's Test
ls.circle           Least Squares Circle
plot.edf            Plot Empirical Distribution Function
plot.ls.circle      Plot Least Squares Circle
pp.plot             von Mises Probability-Probability Plot
pvm                 Cumulative Probability for the von Mises
                      Distribution
r.test              Rayleigh Test of Uniformity:  General Unimodal
                      Alternative
rad                 Radians
rao.homogeneity     Rao's Tests for Homogeneity
rao.spacing         Rao's Spacing Test of Uniformity
rcard               Random Generation from the Cardioid Distribution
rmixedvm            Random Generation from the Mixed von Mises
                      Distribution
rtri                Random Generation from the Triangular Distribution
rvm                 Random Generation from the von Mises Distribution
rwrpcauchy          Random Generation from the Wrapped Cauchy
                      Distribution
rwrpnorm            Random Generation from the Wrapped Normal
                      Distribution
rwrpstab            Random Generation from the Wrapped Stable
                      Distribution
trig.moment         Trigonometric Moments
v0.test             Rayleigh Test of Uniformity:  Alternative with
                      Specified Mean Direction
vm.bootstrap.ci     Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
vm.ml               von Mises Maximum Likelihood Estimates
watson              Watson's Test
watson.two          Watson's Two-Sample Test of Homogeneity
wrpcauchy.ml        Wrapped Cauchy Maximum Likelihood Estimates
==============================================================================

Version 2.0 has the following corrections of bugs and novel features:

*** Corrections

  1. circ.reg:
       In versions of S-PLUS later than 4.5, circ.reg had problems
       b/c the result was not initialized explicitly as a list.
       The result returned by the function is now explicitly initialized
       as a list.  Also, there was an error in the way the function
       assessed whether higher order terms were needed in the
       trigonometric polynomials fit to the data.  In Version 1.0, a
       higher order model was deemed unnecessary if either of the sin or
       cos models did not require a higher order model.  In Version
       2.0,a higher order model is deemed necessary overall if either of
       the sin or cos models are inadequate at a given level.

  2. circ.plot and rose.diag:
       In version 1.0 negative angles were plotted incorrectly.  This
       bug has been corrected.  See further information regarding these
       two functions below.

*** Enhancements/Changes

  1. The "degree" option has been removed from the r.test and v0.test
     functions.  The "rad" (radians) option has been removed from the
     list of possible arguments for the rao.spacing function.  The
     entire library of functions is now consistent in that circular
     arguments are assumed to be measured in radians.

  2. The functions circ.plot and rose.diag have been merged into one
     plotting function, circ.plot.  A rose diagram can now be requested
     as an option. Other options were added for circ.plot, allowing for
     data to be measured in various orientations around the circle, and
     with various 0 directions. Options to affect the labeling and
     points drawn on the plotting device have also been enhanced.

  3. The function nCk has been removed from the library, as S-PLUS now
     has the function choose to perform the same operation. Circ.range
     has been changed to utilize the choose function instead of nCk.

  4. The function circ.aov has been added to the library.  This function
     implements several one-way classification tests for common mean
     directions across several groups of measurements.

  5. The function circ.lin.reg has been added to the library.  This
     function implements the Fisher and Lee (1992) circular/linear
     regression model, predicting a circular response from a set of
     linear covariates.

  6. The function equal.kappa.test has been added to the library.  This
     function implements a test for common concentration parameters
     across several groups of measurements, assuming measurements are
     coming from a von Mises distribution.

  7. The function ls.circle has been added to the library.  This
     function implements a method of computing least squares estimates
     of the parameters of a circle, given a set of measurements in two
     dimensions.  The function plot.ls.circle makes a graph of the data
     with the estimated least squares circle.

===============================================================
Please address questions and comments regarding the library to:

Ulric J. Lund
Department of Statistics
California Polytechnic State University
San Luis Obispo, CA 93407

Email: ulund at calpoly.edu
===============================================================

messages.subject: Re: library call

problem. 

func <- function(libname)

typical repeated measures data format into a "stacked data" format so that you

to:

messages.subject: Re: Calculating p in Minkowsi Distance Formula
messages.subject_clean: Calculating p in Minkowsi Distance Formula
messages.body_plain:
The p's do not cancel, but there is no closed form expression for p, as
far as I can see. What you have is a nonlinear regression problem to
determine the parameter p:

Log(d) = (1/p) . Log[(x1-x2)^p + (y1-y2)^p]

(Note that log(A+B) is not equal to log(A) + log(B) - the most likely
error you made that led to canceling of p.)

You may want to try:

nl.st <- c(p=2) ## look for solutions near p=2, the usual physical
metric.
mink.nl <- nls(formula, start=nl.st, trace=T)

Where formula is the above formula expressed appropriately in S-Plus
format.

Hope that helps.

Nikhil
_________________________________________________
N. S. Padhye, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor & Biostatistician
The University of Texas School of Nursing at Houston
http://www.uth.tmc.edu

Distance formula for p:

d = [(x1-x2)^p + (y1-y2)^p]^1/p

I have D, x1, x2, y1, y2 for about 1300 observations, I want to know the
value of p. When I take Logrithms, p cancels out.

Any suggestion?

Rizwan

The p's do not cancel, but there is no closed form expression for p, as
far as I can see. What you have is a nonlinear regression problem to
determine the parameter p:

Log(d) = (1/p) . Log[(x1-x2)^p

Hello all, Thanks to 
Jean Adams  jvadams at usgs.gov 
Peter Alspach PAlspach at hortresearch.co.nz 
Richard M. Heiberger rmh at temple.edu
and Robert Garrett garrett at NRCan.gc.ca 

for their quick and consistent responses to my query for the per mil symbol 
"0/00". All directed me to the ascii character \211, generally available in the 
form: plot(1:10, main= paste('*', "\211")).
Mr Garrett also kindly provided a useful function to display octal codes:

"rg.dsplay.ascii.o" <- 
function()
{
        # Function to display Windows Latin 1 font octal table.  Used to
        # identify octal codes, e.g., \265 for greek mu, for use in axis
        # titles, etc.
        #
        frame()
        oldpar <- par()
        on.exit(par(oldpar))
        screen(new = T)
        par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2) + 0.10000000000000001)
        v <- 40:377
        v <- v[v %% 100 < 80 & v %% 10 < 8]
        plot(0:7, seq(4, 31, length = 8), type = "n", axes = F, xlab = "",
ylab = "", main = 
                "Windows 3.1 Latin 1 Octal Table")
        k <- 1
        for(i in 4:31)
                for(j in 0:7) {
                        text(j, 35 - i, eval(parse(text = paste("\"\\",
v[k], "\"", sep = ""))))
                        k <- k + 1
                }
        text(0:7, rep(33, 7), as.character(0:7), font = 3)
        text(rep(-1, 28), 31:4, as.character(c(4:7, 10:17, 20:27, 30:37)),
font = 3)
        mtext("Use in S-Plus text strings, e.g., \\265 for mu", side = 1)
        invisible()
}

in the function variogram() and the width with tol.lag. However, that does 
not allow you to have bins of different distances within the same variogram 
(i.e., they have to be equally spaced). I'm not sure if arbitrarily spaced 
bins are possible in Splus and advisable in a statistical sense.

Volker

Your substitute will only work on text files, at least on systems where 
that matters (and dos() only works on a single platform, where it 
does matter).

Your self-imposed restrictions are not widely shared.  In the Unix world
where S comes from, a basic idea is to use combinations of small reusable
tools.  You may possibly be wiser than the computer-science gurus, but I
am afraid your expression of your wisdom is incomprehensible to me.

Incidentally R which was developed in the classic MacOS and Unix and 
Windows worlds simultaneously does have a raft of file.* functions to 
work around OS deficiencies.

When this list had a FAQ it did ask people to mention the platform they 
were using -- that is still a very good idea.

messages.body_plain:
> I used "prompt" to put together the skeleton for a help file for a function.
> 
> I generated the file and went into Notepad and edited the file.
> 
> When I tried to view the file in S +, I got an error message that Xemacs 
> could not be found.
> 
> Why does this happen on new help files, but existing files pull up smoothly, 
> please?
> 
> Thanks in advance.
> 
> S + 6.2 Windows.

I am basing my answer on two things that you wrote.

1. You said you used Notepad to edit the file.  This makes your life
more difficult than using Emacs or Xemacs, but doesn't interfere with
using the help page.

This is easy.  You shouldn't be using Notepad.  You should be using
Emacs or Xemacs.  This is your choice.  Since you are already an Emacs
user, you should use it.

2. You said "Xemacs can't be found".

I use GNU NTemacs, not Xemacs, therefore I am reasonably sure of the
diagnosis and general form of the fix.  I am not sure of the details
of the fix for Xemacs.  Please write back to the list with the exact
fix that works.

Since you get the message "Xemacs could not be found", this suggests that
you have emacsclient set up correctly but do not have Xemacs in your PATH
environment variable.  Let me start by giving the correct fix for NTemacs
and then follow that by the hint for Xemacs.

For NTemacs:
You must install the gnuserv package
  ftp://ftp.gnu.org/old-gnu/emacs/windows/contrib/gnuserv.zip
  ftp://ftp.gnu.org/old-gnu/emacs/windows/contrib/gnuserv.readme.nt
We assume that you have placed "c:/emacs/gnuserv" (this location is
where I place gnuserv.  Use the correct value properly structured for
where you placed it) into your PATH environment variable.

By default, ESS sets the S-Plus options on Windows for pager and help.pager to
gnuclientw.exe and the option for editor to gnuclient.exe.
Therefore, as long as gnuserv is in the PATH, ESS works correctly with no
changes.

For Xemacs:

Since the message you report is looking for Xemacs, this suggests that
emacsclient is set up correctly, but that Xemacs is not in the PATH.
The fix is to put the directory that contains Xemacs.exe into the
PATH.  You can do this with either the
    "control panel"/system/advanced/"environment variables"
or in site-start.el (this assumes you start S-Plus with M-x S).

You also need to set the three S-Plus options
options(editor='emacsclient.exe',
        pager='emacsclient.exe',
        help.pager='emacsclient.exe')
These are probably the right values, but I am not sure.  In
particular, you might need an argument for the pager and help.pager
options.

I have two open questions, for which I need the answers from an Xemacs
user on Windows.
1. Is emacsclient correct?  Is it part of the Xemacs distribution?  Or do you
you need to download it from somewhere (if so, where)?

2. What are the correct values for the three S-Plus options?  Once I
know these values, I will update ESS to automatically turn them on for
Xemacs on Windows.

On your other question
> Why does this happen on new help files, but existing files pull up smoothly, 
> please?
Files you write use a different technology.  The S-Plus supplied help
files are Windows-style help files.  The ones you write are sgml files
and are turned into ascii text and sent to a text editor.

messages.body_plain:
## I see two types of difficulties, one type is actual errors in
## usage, and the other are what I consider less than optimal
## programming style.
##
## Errors
##
## a. The primary errors are indeed in scoping, as you guessed.
## Functions look in the global space for names that they do not find
## inside the current function.  Thus the variable references to j, k,
## d inside the integrand function do not look inside the test
## function for a possible location.  Therefore integrand does not see
## the values in your j and k loops.  The way around that is to give
## integrand a second argument and then use it.  See the revision
## below which fixes all(?) the scoping errors.  Similarly, the test
## function may not see the value of "n".
##
## 
## There are five stylistic issues that contribute to the difficulty in spotting
## the problem.
## 
## b.  I recommend always using " <- " for assignment and never using
## "_".  For comparison, beginning with R 1.9.1, R no longer honors the
## underscore for assignment.
## 
## I think the definition of test with "_" and of integrand with " <- "
## interfered with recognizing that this is a nested set of function 
definitions.
## 
## c. Each level of nesting is not indented within the previous level.
## This makes it hard to see the nesting pattern.
## 
## d. I recommend spaces after all commas.  This makes it easier for people
## to read the code.
##
## e. The integrand function is identical throughout the double loop.
## Therefore I took it out of the loop.  This has two effects.  One is
## that the program will be much more efficient since it only has to
## define the function once.  The other is that it is easier to read,
## hence debug, since the constants are not inside the loop.
##
## f. There is potential danger in using the name "c" for a variable.
## "c" is the name of the catenate function which is used inside every
## S-Plus function.  You run the risk of masking the function and generating
## very untraceable errors.  I changed its name in your function to "cc".

## An additional note, which is probably a consequence of the simplification,
## is that the result of the integration is never used or returned.

## With all this, there is something still wrong.  I get the message
##    Problem in .Fortran("divset",: subroutine divset:
##        Argument 2 has zero length
## I believe the problem is detected inside nlminb, but I can't find it.

## Rich

n <- 5
result <- diag(0,n)

test <- function(b, n) {
  on.exit(browser())
  cc <- b[1]
  d <- b[2]
  integrand <- function(x, j, k, d) {
    sin(x/2)^2/(2*pi*j-x)/(2*pi*k+x)*abs(x/(2*pi*j))^(-2*d)
  }
  for(j in 1:n) {      
    for (k in 1:n) {
      integrate(integrand,
                subdivisions=1000,
                lower=-Inf, upper=Inf,
                j=j, k=k, d=d
                )$integral
    }
  }
  return(cc-exp(d))
}

testout <- nlminb(start=c(0.1,1.0),
                  obj=test,
                  lower=c(0.05,0.5),
                  upper=c(0.45,5.0),
                  n=n)$parameters
testout

----- Original Message -----

Sent: Friday, September 17, 2004 10:08 PM
Subject: RE: [S] Splus NuOpt for S-PLUS Version 1.4.6.3

Steve

I happen to be working on a similar problem...

Your issue is that NUOPT doesn't always get the correct method or parameters
automatically. "Trust" is effective but needs care with initial positions.

Add

nuopt.options(scaling="on", method="asqp", told=1e-10, tolx=1e-10,
eps=1e-10)

before System, and on my machine it seems to solve correctly.

Also I would always define *all* constraints as constraints - or none, and
you seem to have a couple of typo's (q.v. q[i]<-1)

Hope this helps

John James
Insightful

######################################################################

module(nuopt)
initial <- c(0,0,0)
new.model()
I<-Set(1:3)
i<-Element(set=I)
p<-Variable(init=list(1:3, initial), index=I)
q<-Variable(init=list(1:3, initial), index=I)

Sum(p[i],i)==1
Sum(q[i],i)==1

p[i]>=0
p[i]<=1

q[i]>=0

messages.body_plain:
>I hope someone can help me.  I'm trying to do the following:
>
>Let X be an Nxn matrix (n<N).  The rows are people and the columns are 
>their ratings on a product.  I want to create a matrix Z by subtracting 
>each person's mean from their row of X (I can do this using sweep) and 
>then rescaling each row to have sum of squares of one.  Then R = ZZ' is 
>the NxN correlation matrix among the persons.  The matrix Z will be used 
>later for further analysis.
>
>My question: how do I rescale X after sweeping out the means to create Z?

(X - rowMeans(X)) / sqrt( rowVars(X, SumSquares = T))

You can also use sweep(), but that isn't necessary; when doing
        (matrix) (some operation) (vector whose length matches number of rows)
the vector is replicated once for every column of the matrix.

messages.body_plain:
As far as I know there is no analog of setwd().  At startup time you can 
specify the working directory via a command line argument like 
S_PROJ="C:\\Projects\\Data1" (this will affect both the "current directory" 
for file operations, and where S-plus looks for the ".Data" 
directory).  However, I know of no way to change the working directory 
while in a running S-plus session.

-- Tony Plate

messages.subject: More elegant usage of outer?
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to write a nice and elegant function in Splus 6.0 on Windows XP.
Basically what I am trying to do is this:

list1<-1:3
list2<-4:7
list3<-9:12
list4<-0:2

# If I only have list1 and list2
outer(list1,list2,"paste")
# If I have list1, list2 and list3
outer(outer(list1,list2,"paste"),list3,"paste")
# If I have list1, list2, list3 and list4
outer(outer(outer(list1,list2,"paste"),list3,"paste"),list4,"paste")
# And so forth.....

I am thinking there must be a more elegant solution instead of using outer
recursively? It does not matter if the final output is a matrix or array as
long as I can get all the combinations right. I seem to be rather blind at
the moment to see a better solution than the above!

Thank you for your attention.

Steve.

messages.subject: Re: setwd() analogue
messages.body_plain:
There are two distinct interpretations of your question.
Let me try both.

1. Change the .Data that is first on your search() list.
The .Data directory must already exist and you must have write permission.

attach("c:/HOME/tmp/.Data", pos=1)

Now all S-Plus objects that you create by assignment
    a <- 2:5
will be written in c:/HOME/tmp/.Data

2. Change the location where files other than S-Plus objects are
read and written.  In my usual setup,  I start S-Plus from
the c:/HOME/rmh directory and c:/HOME/rmh/.Data is in the first
position of my search() list.  A statement of the form
   myData <- read.table("myData.csv")
will find the file c:/HOME/rmh/myData.csv

I wish to read some data from another location, say from c:/datasets/

Define a function
   datasets <- function(filename) paste("c:/datasets", filename, sep="/")

Then access the file with
   myData <- read.table(datasets("myData.csv"))
This will read the file c:/datasets/myData.csv

The advantage of a function is that it can be changed external to the
read.table statement.  Indeed, it can define a different directory on
every computer you use and still work without changing any code.

My impression of your original question is that you were trying to
solve the second interpretation by a method appropriate to the first
interpretation.

Hui-May_Chu at vrtx.com gave a method similar to the second interpretation.

Tony Plate <tplate at blackmesacapital.com> was suggesting a startup
method equivalent to the first interpretation.

Rich

[I posted this function to R-help a while ago, but should work the same in
S-PLUS.]

gouter <- function(x, FUN, ...) {
  xgrid <- as.list(do.call("expand.grid", x))
  names(xgrid) <- NULL
  array(do.call(deparse(substitute(FUN)), c(xgrid, list(...))),
                dim=sapply(x, length), dimnames=x)
}

messages.body_plain:
The command line variable setting S_PROJ=<dir> actually sets the path 
relative to which file I/O is performed (the original poster's apparent 
question) as well as the location where .Data directory is looked for (and 
also the .Prefs location).  These are independent settings in 
S-PLUS.  These settings can also be controlled independently via the 
command line variables S_CWD, S_DATA, and S_PREFS.  See the "Programmer's 
Guide" for details on all the command line switches: "Chapter 18: The 
S-PLUS Command Line and the System Interface".

Note however that these are completely independent settings -- changing the 
database attached in position 1 has absolutely no effect on the location 
where file(), read.table(), etc. look for files.

-- Tony Plate

messages.body_plain:
That depends on _how_ you want the (pseudo-)random numbers to be distributed
within the range.  If you want uniform (i.e., all numbers within the range
equally likely to be sampled), use something like runif(1000, 1, 41).  If
you want the discrete (i.e., only integers) version, use sample(1:41, 1000,
replace=T).

Andy

Richard has the correct interpretation.  I was trying to avoid using a
function involving "paste", since that's kind of inelegant.

So it looks like, for example, there's no internal commands that lets me
set input directory/ies (e.g. "C:/Projects/Data1"), and then set a
separate output directory/ies (e.g. "C:/Projects/Out"), in any order
and/or frequency (since S_PROJ can only be set only once/session).   Do
I understand correctly?

- Iyue

> -----Original Message-----
> From: Tony Plate [mailto:tplate at blackmesacapital.com]
> Sent: Friday, September 24, 2004 10:16 AM
> To: Richard M. Heiberger; Iyue Sung; s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject: Re: [S] setwd() analogue
> 
> The command line variable setting S_PROJ=<dir> actually sets the path
> relative to which file I/O is performed (the original poster's
apparent
> question) as well as the location where .Data directory is looked for
(and
> also the .Prefs location).  These are independent settings in
> S-PLUS.  These settings can also be controlled independently via the
> command line variables S_CWD, S_DATA, and S_PREFS.  See the
"Programmer's
> Guide" for details on all the command line switches: "Chapter 18: The
> S-PLUS Command Line and the System Interface".
> 
> Note however that these are completely independent settings --
changing
> the
> database attached in position 1 has absolutely no effect on the
location
> where file(), read.table(), etc. look for files.
> 
> -- Tony Plate
> 
> At Thursday 09:25 PM 9/23/2004, Richard M. Heiberger wrote:
> >There are two distinct interpretations of your question.
> >Let me try both.
> >
> >
> >1. Change the .Data that is first on your search() list.
> >The .Data directory must already exist and you must have write
> permission.
> >
> >attach("c:/HOME/tmp/.Data", pos=1)
> >
> >Now all S-Plus objects that you create by assignment
> >     a <- 2:5
> >will be written in c:/HOME/tmp/.Data
> >
> >
> >
> >2. Change the location where files other than S-Plus objects are
> >read and written.  In my usual setup,  I start S-Plus from
> >the c:/HOME/rmh directory and c:/HOME/rmh/.Data is in the first
> >position of my search() list.  A statement of the form
> >    myData <- read.table("myData.csv")
> >will find the file c:/HOME/rmh/myData.csv
> >
> >I wish to read some data from another location, say from c:/datasets/
> >
> >Define a function
> >    datasets <- function(filename) paste("c:/datasets", filename,
> sep="/")
> >
> >Then access the file with
> >    myData <- read.table(datasets("myData.csv"))
> >This will read the file c:/datasets/myData.csv
> >
> >The advantage of a function is that it can be changed external to the
> >read.table statement.  Indeed, it can define a different directory on
> >every computer you use and still work without changing any code.
> >
> >
> >

messages.subject: Seeking advice on PCA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am a newbie at statistics and am trying to learn about principal 
component (PC) analysis by reading and doing some examples with my 
own data. I am using S-Plus (6.2 for Windows) for my analyses.

I have a dataframe (I think that's the right terminology) "mydat" 
with various "columns" x1,x2,x3,x4,x5,x6 for which I am trying to 
compute the principal components.

I use the following command to carry out the analysis:

princomp(x =  ~ x1 + x2 + x3 +x4 + x5 + x6, data = mydat, scores = 
T, cor = T, na.action = na.exclude)

>From looking at output, I can get an idea of which PCs are 
explaining a certain percent of the variance. I can also get 
S-plus to predict the PCs for each "row" in the dataframe.

My question is "How are the individual PCs computed from the base 
properties?" I can look at the loadings and I think these are 
indicative of which properties contribute to which PCs, but I 
don't know how to use this information to compute the actual values.

Are the PCs computed as a linear combination of the properties, e.g.

PC1 = a x1 + b x2 + c x3 + d x4 + e x5 + f x6  ?

If so, how do I get the coefficients?

Thanks for any assistance or advice you can provide.

-g

function(x, y, p) {

p[1] * 
(x/p[2])^(-1/p[3]) - y

function(x, y, p) {

dydp <- matrix(0,

tmp <- 
(x/p[2])^-(1/p[3])

dydp[,1] <- 
tmp

messages.subject: Re: Variable ranking in rpart
messages.body_plain:
1. For a surrogate split, the agreement with the primary split variable is
the number of observations that would be sent the same way (left son,
right son) by the surrogate, as were sent by the primary split.
   One way to think of it is: if the primary variable were hidden from me,
how many correct guesses would I make, using the surrogate?  And you only have
to guess the direction that the primary variable sent the observation, not the
actual value of the primary variable.

 2. The adjusted agreement is the kappa agreement statistic.  Say 80% of the
observations go left (based on the primary split) and 20% go right, and that
the surrogate has an agreement of .93.  A "go with the majority" rule that
sent every obs left would have agreement of .8.  The adjusted agreement is
        (.93 - .8)/(1 - .8) = .65
the fraction of the "potential gain", from .8 to 1, that was achieved.

3. For variable importance, Brieman et al credit each variable with
        improvement, if it is a primary split
        improvement*agreement, if it is not a primary split
        
                Terry Therneau

messages.subject: Re: LME- Comparing likelihood of two models
messages.subject_clean: LME- Comparing likelihood of two models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pravin,

the reason you get this warning is a theoretical one: When you use 
REML you transform your response variable y to y*=t(A)%*%y, in order 
not to having to estimate the fixed-effects beta. Thus the choice of A 
depends each time on the fixed-effects design matrix X. if you have 
two models with different fixed-effects and fit them by REML each one 
has its own Y* and thus when you use anova.lme you compare two models 
with different response variable (not meaningful). On the other hand 
if you use ML instead of REML then you don't transform Y and you just 
need to test nested models. However, it is known that ML gives biased 
results for the variance components since it doesn't take into account 
that you also estimate beta.

For references you could look at

@Article{harville:77,
 author    = {D. Harville},
 journal   = {Journal of the American Statistical Association},
 pages     = {320--340},
 title     = {Maximum likelihood approaches to variance
                   component estimation and to related problems},
 volume    = {72},
 year      = {1977}
}

I hope this helps.

Best,
Dimitris

messages.subject: Re: Sorting dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thom,

you could give a try to the following function:

dat <- data.frame(sex=sample(rep(c("M", "F"), 15)),

                   race=sample(rep(c("W", "B"), 15)),

                   smoking=sample(rep(c("Y", "N"), 15)),

                   weight=rnorm(30, 70))

#####################

sort.data.frame <- function(dat, order){

   if(!is.data.frame(dat)) stop(" `dat' is not a data.frame")

   if(length(order)!=length(dat)) stop(" dimensions of the arguments 
do not match")

   order <- c("asc", "desc")[charmatch(order, c("des", "asc"))]

   dat.a <- dat[,order=="asc"]; dat.a <- sort.col(dat.a, 
names(dat.a))

   dat.d <- dat[,order=="desc"]; dat.d <- sort.col(dat.d, 
names(dat.d), ascending=FALSE)

   dat[,order=="asc"] <- dat.a; dat[,order=="desc"] <- dat.d

   dat

}

sort.data.frame(dat, c("a", "d", "d", "a"))

I hope it helps.

Best,
Dimitris

One of the often asked questions on s-news and r-help relates to sorting
a data frame in ascending/descending order by multiple columns.

I have created a function that does the job very flexibly and in a way that
should be easy to remember.  For example, to sort the Oats data.frame (nlme
library) by nitro (decreasing) and Variety (increasing) :

sort.data.frame(Oats, ~ -nitro + Variety)

Feedback and improvements are welcome.

sort.data.frame <- function(form,dat){
  # Author: Kevin Wright
  # Some ideas from Andy Liaw
  #   http://tolstoy.newcastle.edu.au/R/help/04/07/1076.html

  # Use + for ascending, - for decending.
  # Sorting is left to right in the formula

  # Useage is either of the following:
  # library(nlme); data(Oats)
  # sort.data.frame(~-Variety+Block,Oats) # Note: levels(Oats$Block)
  # sort.data.frame(Oats,~nitro-Variety)

  # If dat is the formula, then switch form and dat
  if(inherits(dat,"formula")){
    f=dat
    dat=form
    form=f
  }
  if(form[[1]] != "~")
    stop("Formula must be one-sided.")

  # Make the formula into character and remove spaces
  formc <- as.character(form[2])
  formc <- gsub(" ","",formc)
  # If the first character is not + or -, add +
  if(!is.element(substring(formc,1,1),c("+","-")))
    formc <- paste("+",formc,sep="")

  # Extract the variables from the formula
  if(exists("is.R") && is.R()){
    vars <- unlist(strsplit(formc,
"[\\+\\-]"))
  }
  else{
    vars <- unlist(lapply(unpaste(formc,"-"),unpaste,"+"))
  }
  vars <- vars[vars!=""] # Remove spurious "" terms

  # Build a list of arguments to pass to "order" function
  calllist <- list()
  pos=1 # Position of + or -
  for(i in 1:length(vars)){
    varsign <- substring(formc,pos,pos)
    pos <- pos+1+nchar(vars[i])
    if(is.factor(dat[,vars[i]])){
      if(varsign=="-")
        calllist[[i]] <- -rank(dat[,vars[i]])
      else
        calllist[[i]] <- rank(dat[,vars[i]])
    }
    else {
      if(varsign=="-")

One of the often asked questions on s-news and r-help relates to sorting
a data frame in ascending/descending order by multiple columns.

I have created a function that does the job very flexibly and in a way that
should be easy to remember.  For example, to sort the Oats data.frame (nlme
library) by nitro (decreasing) and Variety (increasing) :

sort.data.frame(Oats, ~ -nitro + Variety)

Feedback and improvements are welcome.

sort.data.frame <- function(form,dat){  # Author: Kevin Wright
  # Some ideas from Andy Liaw
  #   http://tolstoy.newcastle.edu.au/R/help/04/07/1076.html

  # Use + for ascending, - for decending.
  # Sorting is left to right in the formula

  # Useage is either of the following:
  # library(nlme); data(Oats)
  # sort.data.frame(~-Variety+Block,Oats) # Note: levels(Oats$Block)
  # sort.data.frame(Oats,~nitro-Variety)

  # If dat is the formula, then switch form and dat
  if(inherits(dat,"formula")){    f=dat
    dat=form
    form=f
  }
  if(form[[1]] != "~")
    stop("Formula must be one-sided.")

  # Make the formula into character and remove spaces
  formc <- as.character(form[2])
  formc <- gsub(" ","",formc)
  # If the first character is not + or -, add +
  if(!is.element(substring(formc,1,1),c("+","-")))
    formc <- paste("+",formc,sep="")

  # Extract the variables from the formula
  if(exists("is.R") && is.R()){    vars <- unlist(strsplit(formc,
"[\\+\\-]"))
  }
  else{    vars <- unlist(lapply(unpaste(formc,"-"),unpaste,"+"))
  }
  vars <- vars[vars!=""] # Remove spurious "" terms

  # Build a list of arguments to pass to "order" function
  calllist <- list()
  pos=1 # Position of + or -
  for(i in 1:length(vars)){    varsign <- substring(formc,pos,pos)
    pos <- pos+1+nchar(vars[i])
    if(is.factor(dat[,vars[i]])){      if(varsign=="-")
        calllist[[i]] <- -rank(dat[,vars[i]])
      else
        calllist[[i]] <- rank(dat[,vars[i]])
    }
    else {
      if(varsign=="-")
        calllist[[i]] <- -dat[,vars[i]]
      else
        calllist[[i]] <- dat[,vars[i]]
    }
  }
  dat[do.call("order",calllist),]

}

messages.body_plain:
order(rev(x)) doesn't produce a reversed ordering.  Although order(rev(x)) 
produces something different to order(x), it's not the same (in general) as 
rev(order(x)) (or order(-x) for numeric x).  Also, note that rev(order(x)) 
does not preserve the original ordering of equivalent elements, so it's 
questionable whether this is the right thing to use for a reverse ordering 
of non-numeric vectors.

E.g.:

> x <- c(1,1,2,2)

> order(x)

[1] 1 2 3 4

> order(-x)

[1] 3 4 1 2

> order(rev(x))    # order(rev(x)) "works" in this case

[1] 3 4 1 2

> rev(order(x))    # rev(order(x)) produces a different ordering than 
order(-x) because it orders equivalent elements differently

[1] 4 3 2 1

>

> x <- c(1,4,11,8)

> order(x)

[1] 1 2 4 3

> order(-x)

[1] 3 4 2 1

> rev(order(x))

[1] 3 4 2 1

> order(rev(x))

[1] 4 3 1 2

>

messages.body_plain:
What is the goal of the analysis?  If you want to draw formal inference
(e.g., reporting p-values), it's dangerous to `eyeball' a model from the
data, as that will most likely bias the p-values.

If all you want is a quadratic polynomial, that's not a nonlinear model, and
should be fitted with lm (or lme if you have random effects) with a poly()
term.

Andy

messages.subject: Stacking datasets
messages.body_plain:
How do I put one data.frame 'on top of' another?

That is the new number of rows must equal the sum of the two input data 
frames.

rbind() does exactly this when the datasets match columns.

I need to stack data.frames where the columns don't match completely and 
put missing places where the new column was unavailable before.

A simple example:
top is:
ID WEIGHT
1    66.3
2    52.6

bottom is:

ID  BMI
3      21.6
4       23.1

The combined result should be:
all
ID WEIGHT  BMI
1    66.3          -
2     52.6         -
3    -              21.6
4    -              23.1

Note that 
nrow(all) == nrow(top) + nrow(bottom)

and

columns are the union of the two inputs.

Any suggestions on how to accomplish this would be appreciated.
